claim: Individuals must predict future events to proactively guide their behavior.
source: Individuals must predict future events to proactively guide their behavior.
evidence: This is a general statement about behavior that draws from established understanding in psychology and neuroscience.

claim: Predicting when events will occur is a critical component of temporal expectations.
source: Predicting when events will occur is a critical component of these expectations.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about the importance of temporal prediction in behavior.

claim: Temporal expectations are often generated based on individual cue-duration relationships.
source: Temporal expectations are often generated based on individual cue-duration relationships.
evidence: This reflects established understanding in timing research.

claim: The durations associated with different environmental cues will often co-vary due to a common cause.
source: However, the durations associated with different environmental cues will often co-vary due to a common cause.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposition that forms the basis of the common cause hypothesis.

claim: When the duration associated with one temporal cue changes, timed-responding to other cues shift in the same direction.
source: We show that timing behavior may be calibrated based on this expected covariance, which we refer to as the 'common cause hypothesis'. In five experiments using rats, we found that when the duration associated with one temporal cue changes, timed-responding to other cues shift in the same direction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from five experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Training subjects that expecting covariance is not appropriate in a given situation blocks the cross-cue transfer effect.
source: Furthermore, training subjects that expecting covariance is not appropriate in a given situation blocks this effect.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 4.

claim: Cross-cue transfer in timing behavior is context-dependent.
source: Finally, we confirmed that this transfer is context-dependent.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 5.

claim: Temporal expectations can be guided by local sources of information such as specific environmental stimuli functioning as temporal cues.
source: Temporal expectations can be guided by local sources of information. For example, specific environmental stimuli often function as temporal cues (e.g., a traffic light turning yellow indicates that it will turn red after a certain duration has passed).
evidence: This reflects established knowledge in timing research with an illustrative example.

claim: Global properties of the environment can be used to calibrate temporal expectancies.
source: However, global properties of the environment can be used to calibrate these expectancies.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposition that is tested in the experiments.

claim: In the 8-to-4 group of Experiment 1, decreasing the short cue's duration from 8 to 4 s caused responding to the long (unchanged) cue to shift leftward by -22% ± 5% SEM.
source: Specifically, in the 8-to-4 group, decreasing the short cue's duration from 8 to 4 s caused responding to the long (i.e., unchanged) cue to shift leftward [M = −22% ± 5% SEM, t(9) = −4.10, p<.005; ANOVA: Phase, F(1,8) = 55.72, p<0.001; Cue, F(1,8) = 875.72, p<0.001].
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: In the 16-to-32 group of Experiment 1, increasing the 16 s cue's duration to 32 s caused responding to the short (unchanged) cue to shift rightward by 59% +/- 9% SEM.
source: Likewise, in the 16-to-32 group, increasing the 16 s cue's duration to 32 s caused responding to the short (i.e. unchanged) cue to shift rightward [M = 59% + /- 9% SEM, t(9) = 6.02, p <. 001; ANOVA: Phase, F(1,8) = 49.47, p<0.001; Cue, F(1,8) = 363.02, p<0.001; Phase X Cue, F(1,8) = 68.40, p<0.001].
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: Changes in the spread of responding in Experiment 1 were consistent with the scalar property of interval timing.
source: In other words, changes in the spread of responding were consistent with the scalar property of interval timing, whereby the spread scales in direct proportion to the peak time (Gibbon et al., 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis and references to established timing theory.

claim: The scalar property of interval timing states that the spread scales in direct proportion to the peak time.
source: In other words, changes in the spread of responding were consistent with the scalar property of interval timing, whereby the spread scales in direct proportion to the peak time (Gibbon et al., 1984).
evidence: This is established knowledge in timing research, supported by citation.

claim: During probe trials, rats emit an abrupt burst of responses that typically start before and stop after the expected time of reward.
source: Rather, during probe trials, rats emit an abrupt burst of responses that typically start before and stop after the expected time of reward.
evidence: This describes established behavioral patterns in peak-interval procedures, supported by citation.

claim: In the no-change control group of Experiment 1, peak times did not change reliably and shifted slightly rightward by 6% +/- 5% SEM.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, we did not find reliable transfer to the long (unexposed) cue in this group. Specifically, peak times did not change reliably and, if anything, shifted slightly rightward [M = 6% + /- 5% SEM, t(9) =.86, p>0.05].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Long-cue shifts were larger in the 8-to-4 group than the control group.
source: Furthermore, long-cue shifts were larger in the 8-to-4 group than the control group [ANOVA: Phase X Group, F(1,16) = 16.24, p<.005].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison between groups.

claim: Bayesian analysis showed substantial evidence in favor of the null hypothesis that peak times did not shift during testing in the control group using an uninformative prior.
source: We also ran two Bayesian analyses (see methods) to assess evidence in favor of the null hypothesis that peak times did not shift during testing in the control group. The first used an uninformative prior (i.e. assessing evidence for a non-specific peak time shift). As expected, this showed substantial evidence in favor of the null [Bayes Factor = 3.34].
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian statistical analysis.

claim: Bayesian analysis using a prior testing the specific hypothesis that peak times shifted to the same degree as the 8-to-4 group showed decisive evidence in favor of the null for the control group.
source: Critically, using an alternative prior that tested the specific hypothesis that the peak times shifted to the same degree as the 8-to-4 group showed decisive evidence in favor of the null [Bayes Factor = 2875.88].
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 2, peak times for the unchanged, 16 s cue shifted rightward by 13% +/- 5% SEM when the 8 s cue's duration was increased to 12 s.
source: As depicted in Figure 3B and C, peak times for the unchanged, 16 s cue shifted rightward, consistent with the common cause hypothesis [M = 13% + /- 5% SEM, t(9) = 2.34, p<0.05].
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: The rightward shift in Experiment 2 is consistent with the common cause hypothesis rather than regression to the mean.
source: In this case, the average of all intervals remained to the left of the 16 s cue's duration. Therefore, the regression account predicts a leftward shift in responding. In contrast, according to the common cause hypothesis, increasing the 8 s cue's duration to 12 s should cause responses to the 16 s cue to shift rightward, as the direction of the changed-cue shift should determine the direction of the unchanged-cue shift.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference from the experimental design and results.

claim: In Experiment 3, the magnitude of the long-cue peak time shift was far larger in the change-group (M = −47% ± 4% SEM) than the no-change group (M = −13% ± 8% SEM).
source: Consistent with the common cause hypothesis, the magnitude of the long-cue peak time shift was far larger in the change-group than the no-change group [Figure 4C; Change group: M = −47% ± 4% SEM; t(8) = −7.89, p<0.05; No-change group: M = −13% ± 8% SEM, t(8) = −2.14, p>0.05; ANOVA: Phase X Group, F(1,8) = 16.57, p<0.005; Phase, F(1,8) = 50.33, p<0.001].
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Cue-duration changes produce transfer even when reward structure is controlled for.
source: Collectively, these results provide strong support for the proposal that cue-duration changes produce transfer, even when reward structure is controlled for.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results of Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 4a, transfer to the 8 s cue was observed in the correlated group (M = 13% +/- 5% SEM) and unreliable in the uncorrelated group (M = −6% ± 4% SEM).
source: Consistent with our prediction, transfer to the 8 s cue was observed in the correlated group and, more importantly, unreliable in the uncorrelated group [Figure 5C; Correlated group, M = 13% + /- 5% SEM, t(8) = 2.68, p<0.05; Uncorrelated group, M = −6% ± 4% SEM, t(8) = 1.01, p >. 05; ANOVA: Phase X Group, F(1,8) = 6.81, p<0.05].
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Violating the purported covariance assumption blocks directional transfer to the unchanged cue.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that violating the purported covariance assumption blocks directional transfer to the unchanged cue.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results of Experiment 4a.

claim: In Experiment 4b, medium cue peak time shifts were reliable in the correlated group (M = 53% +/- 22% SEM) and unreliable in the uncorrelated group (M = 5% +/- 3% SEM).
source: Replicating our prior effect, medium cue peak time shifts were reliable in the correlated group and unreliable in the uncorrelated group [Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Correlated group 8 s cue shift, M = 53% + /- 22% SEM, t(8) = 3.5, p<0.05; Uncorrelated group 8 s cue shift, M = 5% + /- 3% SEM, t(8) =.56, p >. 05; ANOVA: Phase X Group, F(1,8) = 6.16, p<0.05].
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The magnitude of the peak-time shift in the correlated group was roughly four times larger in Experiment 4b (M = 53%) compared to Experiment 4a (M = 13%).
source: Importantly, the magnitude of the peak-time shift in the correlated group was roughly four times larger in this experiment (M = 53%), compared to the prior experiment (M = 13%), and more in line with the shift observed in the 16-to-32 group of Experiment 1 (M = 59%).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of experimental results across experiments.

claim: In Experiment 5, short unchanged cue responding shifted in both contexts, but this transfer was attenuated during testing in the no-change context (M = 19% +/- 6% SEM) compared to the change-context (M = 46% +/- 12% SEM).
source: Short, unchanged cue responding shifted in both contexts. Critically, this transfer was attenuated during testing in the no-change context [No-change context shift, M = 19% + /- 6% SEM, t(19) = 3.01, p<0.01; Change-context shift, M = 46% + /- 12% SEM, t(19) = 4.20, p<.005; No-change context shift vs. Change context shift, t(19) = −2.70, p<0.05; ANOVA: Phase X Test Context, F(2,32) = 11.16, p<0.001; Phase, F(2,32) = 65.25, p<0.001; Cue, F(1,16) = 392.28, p<0.001; Phase X Cue, F(2,32) = 37.33, p<0.001].
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Responding to the long, changed cue shifted leftward in the no-change context relative to the peak-times in the change context.
source: Moreover, responding to the long, changed cue also shifted leftward in the no-change context relative to the peak-times in the change context [M = 84% + /- 11% SEM vs. 127% ± 8% SEM from training, respectively; t(19) = −3.31, p<.005], supporting the notion that the temporal expectations for both cues change in a correlated manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: No traditional timing theory can readily account for the findings without modification.
source: As far as we are aware, no traditional timing theory can readily (i.e. without modification) account for our findings.
evidence: This is an inference based on review of existing timing theories.

claim: Established models of timing at both the cognitive and neural level typically assume that the temporal expectations associated with different cues are independent of one another.
source: For example, established models of timing at both the cognitive (Gibbon et al., 1984; Killeen and Fetterman, 1988; Kirkpatrick, 2002; Machado et al., 2009) and neural level (Matell and Meck, 2004; Simen et al., 2011) typically assume that the temporal expectations associated with different cues are independent of one another.
evidence: This is a characterization of existing timing models supported by citations.

claim: Rodents take non-temporal factors into account when guiding responses in time, such as the probability of receiving reward after a given duration.
source: This has been proposed previously and is supported by work showing that rodents take non-temporal factors into account when guiding responses in time, such as the probability of receiving reward after a given duration (Balci et al., 2009; De Corte and Matell, 2016a; Gür and Balcı, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: During Pavlovian conditioning, the learning-rate for a cue is determined by the relative relationship between the duration separating cue-onset and reward-delivery and the interval separating successive rewards.
source: Furthermore, during Pavlovian conditioning, the learning-rate for a cue is determined by the relative relationship between the duration separating cue-onset and reward-delivery and the interval separating successive rewards, rather than the cue-reward interval alone (Balsam and Gallistel, 2009; Gallistel and Balsam, 2014; Gallistel and Gibbon, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Taatgen and van Rijn (2011) proposed a modified clock-memory model based on the ACT-R cognitive architecture that predicted aspects of cross-cue transfer.
source: There is one model that is important to discuss, as it was able to predict aspects of the data where traditional models failed. Specifically, Taatgen and van Rijn (2011) recently proposed a modified clock-memory model based on the well-established ACT-R cognitive architecture, a theory that has enjoyed wide success at explaining cognitive phenomena across a variety of domains (Anderson, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In the ACT-R pooled memory model, the 'temporal memory' associated with a cue is determined by a pool of recently experienced intervals that consists of intervals associated with all cues an observer has experienced in the recent past.
source: In their model, the 'temporal memory' associated with a cue is determined by a pool of recently experienced intervals. Importantly, this pool consists of intervals associated with all cues an observer has experienced in the recent past.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of a specific model from cited work.

claim: Taatgen and van Rijn documented cross-cue transfer in humans similar to the transfer observed in the current study.
source: In support of this, they documented cross-cue transfer in humans, similar to the transfer we observed.
evidence: This claim references findings from cited prior work.

claim: Temporal and episodic memory may be highly inter-related processes.
source: Interestingly, in their model, temporal memories are treated as declarative knowledge, and this proposition was recently supported by work in mice showing that temporal and episodic memory may be highly inter-related processes (Kheifets et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Declarative memory retrieval is heavily influenced by physical context.
source: Work in other domains has shown that declarative memory retrieval is heavily influenced by physical context (Bilodeau and Schlosberg, 1951; Godden and Baddeley, 1975; Smith and Vela, 2001), and ACT-R has been equipped to deal with such contextual variables in the past (Anderson, 1996; Anderson et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Evidence suggests that dimensions such as time and number rely on common-coding mechanisms.
source: For example, evidence suggests that dimensions such as time and number rely on common-coding mechanisms (Brannon et al., 2007; Gallistel and Gelman, 2000; Leibovich et al., 2017; Meck and Church, 1983; Riemer et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Many have documented correlated interactions between the dimensions of time, space, and number.
source: In support of this, many have documented correlated interactions between the dimensions of time, space, and number (Merritt et al., 2010; Rugani and de Hevia, 2017; Walsh, 2003), such as when larger stimuli are perceived as lasting a longer amount of time than smaller stimuli (De Corte et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Larger stimuli are perceived as lasting a longer amount of time than smaller stimuli.
source: In support of this, many have documented correlated interactions between the dimensions of time, space, and number (Merritt et al., 2010; Rugani and de Hevia, 2017; Walsh, 2003), such as when larger stimuli are perceived as lasting a longer amount of time than smaller stimuli (De Corte et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The 'peak-shift' effect is a phenomenon wherein the generalization gradient for a reinforced stimulus is systematically shifted away from a non-reinforced stimulus.
source: For example, the 'peak-shift' effect, wherein the generalization gradient for a reinforced stimulus is systematically shifted away from a non-reinforced stimulus, is a prominent area of conditioning research (Akins et al., 1981; Cheng et al., 1997; Lynn, 2010; Siegel, 1967).
evidence: This describes an established phenomenon in conditioning research, supported by citations.

claim: The 'acquired equivalence' effect is a phenomenon whereby stimuli that predict the same outcome are treated as more similar than stimuli that predict different outcomes.
source: Furthermore, our findings may relate to the 'acquired equivalence' effect, whereby stimuli that predict the same outcome are treated as more similar than stimuli that predict different outcomes (Coutureau et al., 2002; Honey and Hall, 1989).
evidence: This describes an established phenomenon in learning research, supported by citations.

claim: All procedures accorded with Villanova University's Animal Care and Use Committee guidelines (IACUC, protocol 1880) and the Declaration of Helsinki.
source: All procedures accorded with Villanova University's Animal Care and Use Committee guidelines (IACUC, protocol 1880) and the Declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: 100 naïve, male, Sprague-Dawley rats, who were 2-3 months of age at the start of each experiment were used as subjects.
source: 100 naïve, male, Sprague-Dawley rats, who were 2 – 3 months of age at the start of each experiment were used as subjects.
evidence: This describes the subjects used in the experiments.

claim: Rats were housed in pairs, given free access to water, but food restricted to 85-90% of their free-feed weights, adjusted for growth.
source: Rats were housed in pairs, given free access to water, but food restricted to 85 – 90% of their free-feed weights, adjusted for growth.
evidence: This describes the housing and feeding conditions for the experimental subjects.

claim: Sample sizes for each experiment were determined based on prior studies in which a reliable peak time shift of at least 10-20% was assessed.
source: Rats were randomly assigned to experimental groups, and sample sizes for each experiment (10 at a minimum, with a minimum of 5 rats per subgroup) were determined based on prior studies in which a reliable peak time shift of at least 10–20% was assessed (De Corte and Matell, 2016a; Gooch et al., 2007; Matell and Meck, 2004; Matell et al., 2006).
evidence: This describes the rationale for sample size determination, supported by citations.

claim: When averaged across trials, probe trial responding resembles a Gaussian curve with a peak centered over the trained time of reward.
source: When averaged across trials, probe trial responding resembles a Gaussian curve with a peak (i.e. peak time) centered over the trained time of reward, providing an estimate of the temporal expectation associated with the cue in question (for examples see Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the characteristic response pattern in the peak-interval procedure.

claim: In the 16-to-32 group of Experiment 1, both start and stop times were delayed during unchanged cue trials relative to initial training.
source: Specifically, in the 16-to-32 group, both start and stop times were delayed during unchanged cue trials, relative to initial training [Start: M = 59% + /- 12% SEM, t(9) = 4.14, p<.005; Stop: M = 65% + /- 10% SEM, t(9) = 6.23, p<0.001].
evidence: This claim is supported by single-trial analysis of experimental data.

claim: In the 8-to-4 group of Experiment 1, long cue stop times were leftward shifted by -27% ± 5% SEM.
source: Comparably, in the 8-to-4 group, long cue stop times were leftward shifted [M = −27% ± 5% SEM, t(9) = −5.54, p<0.001].
evidence: This claim is supported by single-trial analysis of experimental data.

claim: In the 8-to-4 group of Experiment 1, start times were not reliably different between training and testing.
source: However, start times were not reliably different [M = −4% ± 12% SEM, t(9) = −0.83, p>0.05].
evidence: This claim is supported by single-trial analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 2, there was a marginally significant rightward shift in start times (M = 18% +/- 10% SEM) and a reliable rightward shift in stop times (M = 9% +/- 3% SEM) for the unchanged cue.
source: Finally, there was a marginally significant rightward shift in start times and a reliable rightward shift in stop times [Start, M = 18% + /- 10% SEM, t(9) = 2.02, p=0.075; Stop, M = 9% + /- 3% SEM, t(9) = 2.91, p<0.05].
evidence: This claim is supported by single-trial analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 3, single-trial analyses revealed a significant leftward shift in change-group start times and no reliable shift in the no-change group.
source: Single-trial analyses revealed similar patterns, with a significant leftward shift in change-group start times and no reliable shift in the no-change group, although the difference between groups was only marginally significant in this case [Change group: M = −33% ± 5% SEM, t(8) = −3.27, p<0.05; No-change group: M = −4% ± 11% SEM, t(8) = −0.34, p>0.05; Change vs. No-change group, t(8) = −1.90, p=0.094].
evidence: This claim is supported by single-trial analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 3, stop times were reliably shifted in both the change group (M = −46% ± 4% SEM) and no-change group (M = −19% ± 5% SEM).
source: Stop times were reliably shifted in both groups, suggesting reward structure changes alone may have some impact on timed responding [Change group, M = −46% ± 4% SEM, t(8) = −10.14, p<0.001; No-change group, M = −19% ± 5% SEM, t(8) = −4.12, p<.005].
evidence: This claim is supported by single-trial analysis of experimental data.

claim: Changes in overall reward structure can contribute to some degree of the shift in responding.
source: Collectively, these results provide strong support for the proposal that cue-duration changes produce transfer, even when reward structure is controlled for. However, given the stop-time effect in the no-change group, we cannot rule-out that changes in overall reward structure can contribute to some degree of the shift in responding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results of Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 4a, single-trial analyses showed start and stop time shifts were significant in the correlated group and unreliable in the uncorrelated group.
source: Finally, single-trial analyses agreed with the peak time patterns, with start and stop time shifts being significant in the correlated group [Start, M = 21% + /- 7% SEM, t(8) = 3.44, p<0.01; Stop, M = 12% + /- 4% SEM, ts(8) = 3.5, p<0.01] and unreliable in the uncorrelated group [Start, M = 1% + /- 5% SEM, t(8) =.15, p>0.05; Stop, M = −3% ± 4% SEM, t(8) = −0.78, p>0.05].
evidence: This claim is supported by single-trial analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 4b, single-trial analyses showed rightward shifts in start and stop times were significant in the correlated group and unreliable in the uncorrelated group.
source: Finally, single-trial analyses agreed with the peak time patterns, with rightward shifts in start and stop times being significant in the correlated group [Start, M = 63% + /- 30% SEM; Stop, M = 47% + /- 19% SEM; ts(8) > 3.5, ps <0.01] and unreliable in the uncorrelated group [Start, M = 6% + /- 4% SEM; Stop, M = 15% + /- 7% SEM; ts(8) <.4, ps >0.05].
evidence: This claim is supported by single-trial analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 5, short-cue start times were rightward shifted in both the no-change context (M = 38% +/- 10% SEM) and change-context (M = 68% +/- 21% SEM).
source: Specifically, short-cue start times were rightward shifted in both contexts, relative to training [No-change context, M = 38% + /- 10% SEM, t(19) = 3.60, p<.005; Change-context, M = 68% + /- 21% SEM, t(17) = 3.35, p<.005].
evidence: This claim is supported by single-trial analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 5, short-cue stop times were rightward shifted in the change context (M = 46% +/- 12% SEM) but not reliably shifted in the no-change-context (M = 10% +/- 7% SEM).
source: Short-cue stop times were also rightward shifted in the change context, relative to training [M = 46% + /- 12% SEM, t(17) = 3.80, p<.005], and notably, not reliably shifted in the no-change-context [M = 10% + /- 7% SEM, t(19) = 1.10, p>0.05].
evidence: This claim is supported by single-trial analysis of experimental data.

claim: The common cause hypothesis proposes that observers can benefit from the statistical property that durations associated with distinct temporal cues often covary due to a common underlying cause.
source: The underlying premise of the common cause hypothesis is that common causal factors can often produce covariance among the durations associated with distinct temporal cues. According to this hypothesis, observers can benefit from this statistical property by anticipating that, when the duration associated with one temporal cue changes, the durations associated with other cues will have changed in the same direction.
evidence: This is the theoretical framework proposed by the authors.

claim: The peak-interval procedure involves trials that begin with the presentation of a cue that indicates reward can be earned for responding after a specified duration elapses.
source: We tested this hypothesis using the 'peak-interval' procedure. In this task, trials begin with the presentation of a cue that indicates reward can be earned for responding after a specified duration elapses (e.g. responding at a nosepoke after 16 s have passed).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure used.

claim: Probe trials in the peak-interval procedure are trials in which the cue remains on for much longer than normal and no reward is provided.
source: Probe trials are also included in which the cue remains on for much longer than normal (e.g. 48 –64 s) and no reward is provided.
evidence: This describes a component of the experimental procedure.

claim: Rats in Experiments 1, 2, and 5 were run in 2 hr sessions during the light cycle.
source: Rats in Experiments 1, 2, and 5 were run in 2 hr sessions during the light cycle, while rats in Experiment 3 – 4 were run for 12 hr sessions during their dark cycle to accelerate completion of the experiment, due to the increased complexity of training (see below).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedures.

claim: Rats in Experiments 3-4 were run for 12 hr sessions during their dark cycle to accelerate completion of the experiment.
source: Rats in Experiments 1, 2, and 5 were run in 2 hr sessions during the light cycle, while rats in Experiment 3 – 4 were run for 12 hr sessions during their dark cycle to accelerate completion of the experiment, due to the increased complexity of training (see below).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedures and rationale.

claim: Three rats in Experiment 5 did not show any trials that met the criteria for being included in the single trial analysis.
source: Three rats in Experiment 5 did not show any trials that met our criteria for being included in the single trial analysis (>2 responses and a start and stop time that occurred before and after the peak time, respectively). In those cases, they were omitted when computing the averages and statistics.
evidence: This describes data exclusion criteria and procedures.
